ideas.title: Second Pick Wins
ideas.pitch: A visitor picks a three-flip coin pattern, a smug bot picks its own after seeing it, and a flip-by-flip race decides whose pattern shows up first. Every first pick loses at least two thirds of the time to the best reply, so the visitor runs ten million simulated races and watches the bot's edge settle on exact fractions such as 2 to 1. Then the visitor takes the second pick and the table flips; a red-and-black card mode with tricks shows the same effect in a real deck.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. The game is fair in each pick yet decided by the order of choosing, which makes it a durable argument-loser.

research.summary: In Penney's game two players each pick a short heads-tails pattern and the one that appears first in a fair coin sequence wins. Because picking is sequential, the second picker can answer any three-flip pattern with a reply that is strictly more likely to appear first (at least 2 to 1 for length 3, computed here from the leading-number formula). A short rule builds the reply, and Conway's leading-number method gives exact odds. A red/black card version with tricks (Humble-Nishiyama) exists. The page can show the payoff matrix for lengths 3 to 5, exact odds next to a seeded Monte Carlo, and expected waiting times. At length 3 the winning reply never has a longer average wait than the pattern it beats, but at length 4 it can (THTH, wait 20, beats HTHH, wait 18, with probability 9/14), which is where the loss feels unfair.

ideas.title: Clause And Effect
ideas.pitch: The visitor is the lone clerk of an Amendments Desk facing a knot of red tape: offices drawn as nodes, requirements as strands, and queues of citizens stuck because permit A needs B and B needs A. With a small budget of amendment clauses (an exemption, a sunset clause, a grandfather clause, a deemed-approved-after-N-days rule) the visitor pulls strands loose and then runs a simulated crowd through the system, watching who still gets stuck. Side effects in the spirit of Parkinson's satire punish lazy fixes, since every new office spawns paperwork for its neighbours, so the tidiest unravelled desk wins.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. It turns a real piece of computer science (deadlock and circular wait) into a joke-rich puzzle that rewards seeing the structure of a mess.

research.summary: Operating-systems course notes describe deadlock as needing four conditions together (mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait), and say prevention works by breaking any one of them. Where each resource has a single instance, a cycle in the resource-allocation or wait-for graph means deadlock; with several instances a cycle only signals possible deadlock. That gives the puzzle a precise rule: every permit is a single-instance resource, so a strongly-connected-component pass can show the player exactly which knot is the Catch-22. Catch-22 (Heller, 1961) is the cultural name for a trap of mutually dependent or conflicting rules. Parkinson's satire of bureaucratic growth (essay 1955, book 1958) supplies the idea that offices make work for each other, which is the side-effect rule that stops brute-force fixing. All offices, permits and citizens are invented, and any growth rate shown on the page is an invented number labelled as fiction.

ideas.title: The Overtoaster
ideas.pitch: The product page, control panel and manual of an invented heater-grid toaster that burns pictures onto bread, with a real two-stage heat and moisture simulation underneath. The visitor sets power per heating cell, watches the slice dry out first and only then brown, and tries to match a daily target design without charring the crust, while the product's absurd subscription tiers and pop-ups pester the page in the margins. The finished slice is a screenshot-ready piece of burnt art with a deadpan review.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. Appliances that hide features behind paywalls and apps are a lasting genre to lampoon, and a toaster is the oldest joke in connected gadgets.

research.summary: Search re-checks agree on the physics that shapes the mechanic: bread surface water holds the surface near or below 100 C, so toasting is a drying stage followed by a browning stage. Sources disagree on when browning starts (about 120 to 150 C in a patent summary, about 140 C in a science explainer, above about 155 C in an encyclopedia article), so the sim uses a labelled toy band. Patents and older gadgets already print or select browning patterns, including heat-blocking plates and a PC-connected 2008 concept, so the page is a genre parody and not a novelty claim. Press and commentary pages describe hardware features moved behind subscriptions (a car-maker garage opener, a baby bassinet), which grounds the tier-and-pop-up satire; the page targets the practice and names no company.

ideas.title: Jokers In Phase
ideas.pitch: A fan-made concept sandbox for a poker roguelike: a new joker family whose bonuses depend on timing instead of just position. A Pendulum joker swings between flat mult and multiplied mult hand by hand, Firefly jokers blink on their own beat and slowly nudge their neighbours into step, and Handshake jokers pay out only when the two jokers beside them are in matching phase. The visitor arranges a five-slot rail, plays seeded hands through a tiny chips-times-mult engine with play-money chips, and watches a phase ring show who is in sync; a fully synchronised rail makes the whole page pulse once and drops a shareable concept card.
ideas.whyNow: Joker ordering is a well-known puzzle in the genre, and this family adds a timing axis to it. The page is a self-contained sandbox that works offline, so it stays good for weeks.

research.summary: Community guides agree on the evaluation rule that makes joker order matter: effects resolve left to right, so flat mult added early is multiplied by later multiplying jokers. Two guides give worked examples (one doubles mult before a +16 and ends at 26 instead of 42). That ordering is the hook the new family bends: besides where a joker sits, when it fires also changes its value. Fireflies are a classic case of many weakly coupled rhythms locking together, modelled by the Kuramoto family of coupled phase oscillators; a 2025 APS meeting abstract tests a Kuramoto variant on swarm data. This gives the Firefly joker a real, recomputable rule. Modding in this scene commonly uses the Steamodded framework with the Lovely injector, which is background only; the page ships no mod files. All scoring numbers in the page are invented for the concept and labelled as such. One forum user reported seeing multipliers apply regardless of order, without a controlled test; the page states the left-to-right rule as the guides' description, not as a developer statement.

ideas.title: The Waiting Hum
ideas.pitch: A calm little waiting room whose arrivals and departures are played as soft notes: run it at low load and it sounds like a slow lullaby, push the load toward capacity and the tune swells, stutters and collapses into a tangle. The visitor staffs the counters, chooses one shared line or separate lines, and tunes how erratic arrivals and service are, trying to keep the average wait under a target on a budget. A live panel compares the running simulation with the textbook formulas, so the famous knee in the waiting-time curve is something you hear and see.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. Queue theory is the textbook definition of a dud subject, rescued by letting the visitor hear a system approach saturation.

research.summary: Search results from several independent course and reference pages agree on the M/M/1 results (mean number in system rho/(1-rho), mean time 1/(mu-lambda), both growing without bound as utilization approaches 1) and on Little's law linking number, rate and time. Kingman's approximation adds a variability term that lets the page show why erratic arrivals or service inflate waits; it is best near saturation and weaker for very bursty arrivals. Erlang C is the standard multi-server delay model (Poisson arrivals, exponential service, no abandonment). Whether one pooled line beats separate lines is not settled for human servers: the simple model favours pooling, while a Penn Today summary of research on strategic servers describes a case where dedicated queues did better, so the page treats pooling as a result of its own simulation with fixed-speed servers and says so. Parameter-mapping sonification is an established technique, and quantizing to a musical scale trades resolution for musicality. The simulation computes truth; the formulas run alongside as a check.

facts.claim: An M/M/1 queue is stable only when arrival rate is below service rate (utilization below 1); mean number in system is rho/(1-rho) and mean time in system is 1/(mu-lambda), and both grow without bound as utilization approaches 1.
Little's law (mean number equals arrival rate times mean time) is the step that turns the M/M/1 mean number into the mean time in system.

Kingman's approximation puts the mean wait in a G/G/1 queue near rho/(1-rho) times half the sum of the squared variability of arrivals and of service times, times the mean service time; it is accurate near saturation and exact for Poisson arrivals, with accuracy degrading for very bursty arrivals.
Erlang C is the M/M/c delay model: Poisson arrivals, exponential service times and no abandonment, with stability requiring offered load below the number of servers.

For identical servers working at a fixed speed, a single line feeding all servers is described as reducing the chance of being stuck behind a slow customer and balancing load across servers; this is the qualitative effect the simulation will show, not a measured claim about real shops.
Parameter-mapping sonification assigns data values to pitch, and quantizing to a musical scale trades resolution for musicality and can create an effect unrelated to the data.

facts.claim: Papers, Please is a 2013 document-checking game by Lucas Pope (released 2013-08-08 for PC and Mac) in which the player compares travelers' papers with a rulebook and decides who is admitted.

Per a Game Developer feature, Papers, Please asks the player to process as many travelers as possible each day while admitting only those with documents in order, and Lucas Pope said the bureaucratic setting made it easy to fill out a complex set of gameplay rules.

The term Catch-22 comes from Joseph Heller's 1961 novel: a pilot who asks to be grounded as insane shows he is sane by asking, so cannot be grounded; it now means a trap of mutually dependent conditions.

Official and legal papers were bound with red tape in the 17th century; Phrase Finder and Word Origins both cite a Maryland law from 1696 (Phrase Finder gives the range 1696 to 1715) as the earliest literal reference found.
Government clerks used a narrow dyed cotton or linen ribbon called red tape to tie bundles of papers and to seal documents, per the US National Archives.

As of 2026-10-10, per an itch.io listing seen in one search result, a 2017 jam prototype called Ministerio Simulator has up to four local players picking up, stamping and copying forms for a front desk (reported, single result, not confirmed).

design.coreLoop: The citizen reads a small rulebook (each counter: needs, stamps, closing time, queue length, one human quirk), plans a route on a floor map, then walks it, spending clock time, patience and biscuits. Wrong windows, lunch closures and circular requirements force replanning, and combining rules produces loopholes the built-in solver recognises and names. A run ends in a stamped receipt scored on time, patience and loopholes found; a fresh seed or the daily seed restarts it with a different ministry.

Shareable route receipt drawn with SVG tilted ink stamps and procedural WebAudio thumps, plus a loophole journal that persists in localStorage
Every rule carries a human-warmth joke: clerks relax for cake, a stamp is waived if the visitor asks after a cat, the underpass is kept open by a night-shift tea trolley

ideas.title: Seven Riffles
ideas.pitch: A night-shift dealer swears three riffles is plenty. The visitor cuts a 52-card deck and releases a riffle, watches the rising sequences fan out like strands, and sees a meter of how far the whole riffle process still sits from a truly random deck, computed exactly on the page. Then an audit runs thousands of seeded shuffles at 1 to 10 riffles and charts which simple tests (top card, suit runs, card guessing) stop betraying the opening order, and when.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: the seven-shuffles slogan is half-known, and which yardstick you pick changes the verdict, which makes it a good argument to lose.

research.summary: The Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model cuts a deck at a binomially distributed point and interleaves the two piles with probability proportional to pile sizes. Bayer and Diaconis showed that the chance of any deck order after m riffles depends only on its number of rising sequences r, as C(2^m + n - r, n) / 2^(mn), so the distance from uniform for 52 cards can be computed exactly by grouping orders by r (Eulerian counts) and compared with Monte Carlo. Total variation distance stays near 1 at five riffles, is about 0.924 at five, 0.614 at six and 0.334 at seven, so the slogan comes from a drop below one half at seven. A report of work by the Trefethens says an information-style yardstick would accept five to six; that is a single report, so the page treats it as attributed, not established. The page computes its own numbers and labels them as computed here. 52 factorial is about 8.07e67.

facts.claim: For a 52-card deck under the Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model, total variation distance from uniform is about 0.924 after five riffles, 0.614 after six and 0.334 after seven.
The distance stays close to 1 through five riffles and falls below one half only at seven riffles, which is where the seven-shuffles slogan comes from.
The number of orderings of a 52-card deck is 52 factorial, about 8.0658e67.

After m riffles of an n-card deck, the probability of an arrangement with r rising sequences is C(2^m + n - r, n) / 2^(mn), so it depends only on r and exact distances can be computed without sampling.

As of 2026-10-10, per Science News, the Trefethens argued that five riffles do a reasonable job and six make mixing practically certain, using an information-style yardstick (single report, unverified).

The practical exposure is look-alike trade dress (green felt, blue chips with red mult, CRT shader, pixel art, card backs) and the game's name in the title or thumbnail. -> Visible unofficial-fan-concept line in the first viewport, the name used only there, in the About panel and in tags, an original visual identity, invented numbers and glyphs, no game vocabulary, system fonts only (mustFixInSpec items 4 and 5).

The real cost is tuning and testing, not typing, and a spec that quietly shrinks to a mini-spec mismatches build and QA (premortem FM-83, the risk that sits in my lane today). -> SPEC header states tier 1, a per-file line budget and an ordered cut list that leaves a valid core (mustFixInSpec item 16), so a scope-cut directive removes list items instead of forcing a rewrite.

ECMA-262 only requires Math.sin and its relatives to be implementation-approximated, and search results report last-bit differences between engines (one open issue reports a simulation diverging between Node 20 and a recent Chrome, unverified). mustFixInSpec: 1. FACTS POLICY for the About panel. Only these third-party statements appear, each dated 'as of 2026-10-10': (a) community guides (Destructoid, Prima Games) describe joker effects as resolving left to right, with exceptions for effects that fire when a card scores, and one uncontrolled forum report disagrees; (b) the Kuramoto model is the textbook toy for coupled phase oscillators (Complexity Explorables, 'ride my kuramotocycle'); (c) a 2025 APS March Meeting abstract, 'Relating the Kuramoto model to data from immobile firefly swarms', relates a Kuramoto variant to flash data from one firefly swarm; (d) optional: pulse-coupled models (Mirollo and Strogatz, SIAM 1990) are the other classic way to model fireflies, no link needed. Never write that fireflies 'are' Kuramoto oscillators. State that the engine is a simplified concept with invented numbers, and name authors only if a search result you saw shows them.

2. NO THIRD-PARTY NUMBERS. Do not reproduce the 26-versus-42 or the 6,966 examples or credit any guide for a worked example (the dossier's Prima Games attribution of 26 versus 42 is unsupported; my searches point to Inverse and no guide host would open). Show the page's own computed left-to-right example, tagged 'computed by this page'. Do not use the real game's base chips and mult table: choose distinct invented numbers so the 'invented' label is true.

3. SOURCE LIST: at most 5 links (Destructoid, Prima Games, the APS abstract, Complexity Explorables, and the Steamodded repository only if modding is mentioned at all). Drop Nexus Mods pages 887 and 909 (never opened, third-party mod pages), the Mistigris, Community College Pack, Blueprint/Brainstorm and abakcus entries, and the Georgia Tech PDF. Say 'search-only' where that is the evidence. Do not claim the idea is new to the genre: a vanilla joker with a hands-played cycle exists (Loyalty Card, X4 every 6th hand, per several search results).

4. LABELS AND TRADE DRESS. One visible line in the first viewport at 360x640 and 1280x800, for example: 'Unofficial fan concept in the style of joker-deck roguelikes such as Balatro. Not affiliated with or endorsed by its developer or publisher. No game art, fonts, logos or audio are used; numbers and art are invented.' The game's name appears only there, in the About panel, in project.json and in tags, never in the H1, the document title or large display text. Own visual identity: no CRT or scanline shader, no pixel art, no green felt, no blue-chips/red-mult colour pairing, no card-back pattern, no mascot, system font stack only. Avoid the game's own vocabulary (Blind, Ante, Voucher, Tarot, Planet, Spectral, Stake); use 'target' and 'par'.

5. NO WAGER VOCABULARY. Chips are score points. One line near the score: 'Chips here are score points, not money: nothing is bet, bought or won.' Ban bet, wager, ante, payout, pay out, jackpot, cash, coin, buy, shop, reroll and any currency symbol in UI copy, tooltips, the concept card and project.json; write 'adds' or 'scores' instead of 'pays out'.

6. POKER EVALUATOR. Define the categories (standard poker has nine: high card, pair, two pair, three of a kind, straight, flush, full house, four of a kind, straight flush; the dossier says eight, so say which is dropped and why). Ace plays high or low in a straight (A-2-3-4-5 counts, no wrap-around). Ship a headless Node test that enumerates all 2,598,960 five-card hands and asserts exactly: straight flush 40 (4 of them royal), four of a kind 624, full house 3,744, flush 5,108, straight 10,200, three of a kind 54,912, two pair 123,552, pair 1,098,240, high card 1,302,540 (flush and straight exclude straight flushes). I verified these by enumeration.

7. DETERMINISM. All randomness through the seeded mulberry32 (Math.random only for decoration); phases are integers (for example 0 to 1023 ticks per turn), coupling reads a literal integer sine table, and nothing that touches state or score calls Math.sin, cos, exp, pow or log (ECMA-262 leaves their results implementation-approximated; trig is for drawing only). Put 3 golden hash states with exact expected scores in the headless test and in the browser check.

8. SOLVABILITY BY CONSTRUCTION. The engine is a pure function (state, action) to (state, trace); the log and cascade render the trace and never recompute. A solver brute-forces every rail for the current seed (if the rail is set once, a few thousand arrangements, milliseconds; if it can be rearranged each hand, use a bounded beam search and call its output 'a working line', not 'the best'). Each shipped challenge uses a seed from a build-time search with a known par and a small share (roughly 1 to 10 percent) of rails reaching the lock; hash seeds outside the vetted set show 'best rail locks n of 3' and offer the next vetted seed; a hint button after three misses reveals one working rail.

9. DEPTH ACCEPTANCE (headless, per shipped challenge; thresholds are starting points): par is reachable; the best score is at least 1.5x the median rail; at least two distinct near-optimal rails exist; the best rail differs between at least two challenges; the best rail for the lock is not simply the best rail for left-to-right mult (state the tension). The SPEC must say whether the rail is set once or rearranged between hands, what minute ten teaches, how many jokers are in the pool (at least 8 for 5 slots), and use distance-decaying coupling so placements are not reduced to 7 adjacency patterns. Also define Handshake at the rail ends, the matching-phase tolerance including Pendulum versus Firefly, empty slots, and what happens after the last hand.

10. COUPLING KNOB is not a free slider. Fixed per challenge, or priced (stronger coupling reduces each Firefly's flash bonus), or three detents; in free sandbox mode it may be free but the full-sync reward is withheld.

11. PHASE DISPLAY AND FIRST FRAME. The ring and table show the phases that will score on the NEXT hand (a preview); animation only interpolates between discrete states and never shows a state the engine will not score. The first frame is a pre-played demo hand (ring, cascade and score visible) and sets window.__sedThumbReady. The phase ring sits on a dark 'night' panel in both colour schemes because the thumbnail is a light-mode screenshot.

12. FIRST MINUTE AND REWARD LADDER, in plain words for visitors who never played the game. 0 to 10 s: one-line premise and one glowing Play button. 10 to 30 s: guided hand with chips times mult explained. 30 to 50 s: prompt to swap two jokers and watch the score change. 50 to 70 s: first par reached with one swap. Fireflies arrive in challenge 2, Handshake in challenge 3. A full lock gives the gold concept card and one slow glow; two of three gives a silver card; the card preview and copy-link are available at any time.

13. HASH AND STATE SAFETY. Parse the hash with a whitelist (joker ids from an enum, integers clamped, unknown keys ignored), render only enumerated names via textContent, never free text from the hash on the card or in the page (content spoofing); a bad hash falls back to the default state with a small notice; localStorage in try/catch and the page correct without it.

14. INPUT, ACCESSIBILITY, MOBILE. Reordering works by drag, by tap-select then tap-slot or arrow buttons, and by keyboard (Space grabs, arrows move, Enter drops, Escape cancels) with aria-live announcements; five cards fit one row at 360 px (about 56 px each, no horizontal scroll); touch-action none only on the drag handle; the ring has role img with an aria-label updated each hand and a real table (also the reduced-motion view); phase is never encoded by colour alone; suits and joker glyphs are drawn as SVG or canvas paths, not emoji or Unicode card characters (they can render as colour emoji or in a mismatched font).

15. MOTION AND SOUND. The sync pulse is a single glow of at least 600 ms with under 10 percent relative-luminance change, not a flash; Firefly blinks combined stay under 2 per second over any large area; prefers-reduced-motion removes pulse, drift and blinks; audio starts muted, needs a user gesture, and failure to create an AudioContext is silent.

16. SCOPE AND CREDIT (premortem FM-83). The SPEC header states tier 1, a per-file line budget (aim 900 to 1,300 own lines, floor 700) and an ordered cut list that leaves a valid core if a scope-cut arrives: cut PNG export first, then audio, then the third challenge, then the free sandbox mode. Must survive: tested engine, rail with all input paths, ring plus table, cascade log, two solvable challenges, hash state, About panel, labels. Keep the 'Built by the Sonnet Every Day team' credit visible and use abstract geometric joker glyphs drawn in code, no character illustrations.
